Reference: Roth et al. (2023)

Model Setting

The paper synthesizes the recent econometrics literature on difference-in-differences (DiD) and turns it into concrete recommendations for practitioners. It first writes down a set of canonical assumptions under which the econometrics of DiD is well understood: two periods, a treated population that receives a binary treatment in the second period and a comparison population that never does, parallel trends, no anticipation, and a large sample of independent clusters. Under these assumptions the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) is identified, a two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression estimates it consistently, and cluster-robust standard errors give asymptotically valid inference. The paper then classifies the recent literature by which component of this canonical setup is relaxed: (i) multiple periods and variation in treatment timing, (ii) potential violations of parallel trends, and (iii) alternative frameworks for inference. Being a survey, it contains no empirical application; a Medicaid expansion example (state iii, insurance coverage as outcome) is used for illustration only.

The main messages are as follows. With staggered timing and heterogeneous treatment effects, TWFE regressions make forbidden comparisons that use already-treated units as controls, so that some treatment effects enter the TWFE estimand with negative weights; heterogeneity-robust estimators instead use only clean comparisons and aggregate them with weights chosen by the researcher. Parallel trends may hold only conditional on covariates, in which case regression adjustment, inverse probability weighting and doubly robust estimators are available while a linear TWFE specification with covariates can fail. Tests for pre-trends have low power and induce pre-test bias, and should be accompanied by power diagnostics and by sensitivity analyses that bound the post-treatment violation of parallel trends by the pre-treatment violations. With few clusters every available inference method needs some strong additional assumption, and a design-based view implies that standard errors should be clustered at the level at which treatment is independently assigned.

Canonical Two-Period Model

There are two periods t=1,2t=1,2t=1,2 and units i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,Ni=1,…,N. Units from the treated population (Di=1D_i=1Di​=1) receive the treatment between the two periods, and units from the untreated population (Di=0D_i=0Di​=0) remain untreated in both. The econometrician observes a balanced panel of outcomes Yi,tY_{i,t}Yi,t​ and treatment status DiD_iDi​. Let Yi,t(0,0)Y_{i,t}(0,0)Yi,t​(0,0) be the potential outcome of unit iii in period ttt if it is untreated in both periods and Yi,t(0,1)Y_{i,t}(0,1)Yi,t​(0,1) the potential outcome if it is treated by the second period; these are abbreviated to Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​(0) and Yi,t(1)Y_{i,t}(1)Yi,t​(1), but they correspond to paths of treatment. The observed outcome is Yi,t=DiYi,t(1)+(1−Di)Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}=D_iY_{i,t}(1)+(1-D_i)Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​=Di​Yi,t​(1)+(1−Di​)Yi,t​(0). The framework embeds the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): the outcomes of unit iii do not depend on the treatment status of other units, which rules out spillovers and general equilibrium effects. The target parameter is the average treatment effect on the treated in period 2:

τ2=E[Yi,2(1)−Yi,2(0)∣Di=1](1)\tau_2=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(1)-Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1\right] \tag{1}τ2​=E[Yi,2​(1)−Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1](1)

The difficulty is that Yi,2(0)Y_{i,2}(0)Yi,2​(0) is never observed for the treated group. The key identifying assumption (Assumption 1) is parallel trends:

E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=1]=E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=0](2)\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=0\right] \tag{2}E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=1]=E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=0](2)

A model that rationalizes the assumption is Yi,t(0)=αi+ϕt+ϵi,tY_{i,t}(0)=\alpha_i+\phi_t+\epsilon_{i,t}Yi,t​(0)=αi​+ϕt​+ϵi,t​ with ϵi,t\epsilon_{i,t}ϵi,t​ mean-independent of DiD_iDi​. Treatment may then be selected on characteristics that shift the level of the outcome (αi\alpha_iαi​), but not on variables that shift its trend (ϵi,t\epsilon_{i,t}ϵi,t​): selection bias is allowed, but it must be the same in both periods. The second assumption (Assumption 2) is no anticipation: Yi,1(0)=Yi,1(1)Y_{i,1}(0)=Y_{i,1}(1)Yi,1​(0)=Yi,1​(1) for all iii with Di=1D_i=1Di​=1, so that the treatment has no causal effect before it is implemented. For identification it is enough that this holds on average in the treated group.

The identification result is that τ2\tau_2τ2​ is identified under Assumptions 1 and 2. The proof has three steps. Rearranging parallel trends expresses the counterfactual mean of the treated group in period 2 as its untreated mean in period 1 plus the untreated trend of the comparison group. No anticipation replaces Yi,1(0)Y_{i,1}(0)Yi,1​(0) by Yi,1(1)Y_{i,1}(1)Yi,1​(1) for the treated group. Finally, Y(1)Y(1)Y(1) is observed for treated units and Y(0)Y(0)Y(0) for untreated units:

E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=1]=E[Yi,1(1)∣Di=1]+E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=0]=E[Yi,1∣Di=1]+E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0](3)\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]&=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}(1)\mid D_i=1\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=0\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0\right] \end{aligned} \tag{3}E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1]​=E[Yi,1​(1)∣Di​=1]+E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=0]=E[Yi,1​∣Di​=1]+E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0]​(3)

The counterfactual mean of the treated group is therefore its observed pre-treatment mean plus the change in the mean of the untreated group. Subtracting it from the observed mean E[Yi,2∣Di=1]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}\mid D_i=1\right]E[Yi,2​∣Di​=1] gives the difference-in-differences of population means:

τ2=E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=1]−E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0](4)\tau_2=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0\right] \tag{4}τ2​=E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0](4)

Estimation and Inference in the Canonical Model

Replacing expectations by sample analogs gives the DiD estimator:

τ^2=(Y‾t=2,D=1−Y‾t=1,D=1)−(Y‾t=2,D=0−Y‾t=1,D=0)(5)\widehat{\tau}_2=\left(\overline{Y}_{t=2,D=1}-\overline{Y}_{t=1,D=1}\right)-\left(\overline{Y}_{t=2,D=0}-\overline{Y}_{t=1,D=0}\right) \tag{5}τ2​=(Yt=2,D=1​−Yt=1,D=1​)−(Yt=2,D=0​−Yt=1,D=0​)(5)

where Y‾t=t′,D=d\overline{Y}_{t=t',D=d}Yt=t′,D=d​ is the sample mean of YYY for treatment group ddd in period t′t't′. The same number is obtained, together with standard errors, from the two-way fixed effects regression:

Yi,t=αi+ϕt+(1[t=2]⋅Di)β+ϵi,t(6)Y_{i,t}=\alpha_i+\phi_t+\left(1[t=2]\cdot D_i\right)\beta+\epsilon_{i,t} \tag{6}Yi,t​=αi​+ϕt​+(1[t=2]⋅Di​)β+ϵi,t​(6)

which regresses the outcome on a unit fixed effect, a time fixed effect and the interaction of a post-treatment indicator with treatment status. The ordinary least squares coefficient β^\widehat{\beta}β​ equals τ^2\widehat{\tau}_2τ2​. With a balanced panel it is also numerically identical to the interaction coefficient in a regression on a constant, a treatment indicator, a second-period indicator and their interaction, which extends to repeated cross-sections. The sampling assumption (Assumption 3) is that the vectors Wi=(Yi,2,Yi,1,Di)′W_i=(Y_{i,2},Y_{i,1},D_i)'Wi​=(Yi,2​,Yi,1​,Di​)′ are NNN independent and identically distributed draws from a distribution FFF that satisfies parallel trends. Under Assumptions 1 to 3 and mild regularity conditions, as N→∞N\rightarrow\inftyN→∞ with TTT fixed:

N(β^−τ2)→dN(0,σ2)(7)\sqrt{N}\left(\widehat{\beta}-\tau_2\right)\rightarrow_d\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^2\right) \tag{7}N​(β​−τ2​)→d​N(0,σ2)(7)

The paper prints the scaling as the square root of nnn although the sample size is called NNN everywhere else. The variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 is consistently estimated by standard clustering methods that allow arbitrary serial correlation within a unit. The same logic applies when the observations are individuals who belong to independently sampled clusters (for example states) and the standard errors are clustered at that level, provided the numbers of treated and of untreated clusters both grow large.

Staggered Treatment Timing

The first relaxation keeps parallel trends, no anticipation and independent sampling, and allows many periods with units treated at different times. There are TTT periods, t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,Tt=1,…,T, and a binary treatment that can start in any period t>1t>1t>1 and is an absorbing state. Let Di,tD_{i,t}Di,t​ indicate whether unit iii is treated in period ttt, and let Gi=min⁡{t:Di,t=1}G_i=\min\{t:D_{i,t}=1\}Gi​=min{t:Di,t​=1} be the first treated period, with Gi=∞G_i=\inftyGi​=∞ for units never treated in the sample. Units with the same GiG_iGi​ form an adoption cohort; G\mathcal{G}G denotes the set of cohorts. Because treatment stays on, the whole path of treatment is summarized by the starting date, and potential outcomes are written Yi,t(g)Y_{i,t}(g)Yi,t​(g) for a unit first treated in period ggg and Yi,t(∞)Y_{i,t}(\infty)Yi,t​(∞) for the never-treated potential outcome. The simplest generalization of parallel trends (Assumption 4) requires the two-group, two-period version for all pairs of periods and all pairs of cohorts, that is, for all t≠t′t\neq t't=t′ and g≠g′g\neq g'g=g′:

E[Yi,t(∞)−Yi,t′(∞)∣Gi=g]=E[Yi,t(∞)−Yi,t′(∞)∣Gi=g′](8)\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,t}(\infty)-Y_{i,t'}(\infty)\mid G_i=g\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,t}(\infty)-Y_{i,t'}(\infty)\mid G_i=g'\right] \tag{8}E[Yi,t​(∞)−Yi,t′​(∞)∣Gi​=g]=E[Yi,t​(∞)−Yi,t′​(∞)∣Gi​=g′](8)

In the absence of treatment, average outcomes of all cohorts, including the never-treated, would have evolved in parallel. Weaker variants exist. Assumption 4.a (Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021) imposes the same equality only for t,t′≥gmin−1t,t'\geq g_{min}-1t,t′≥gmin​−1, where gmin=min⁡Gg_{min}=\min\mathcal{G}gmin​=minG is the first period in which any unit is treated, so that nothing is imposed on earlier pre-treatment periods. Other versions impose it only among eventually treated cohorts and exclude g=∞g=\inftyg=∞. Stronger versions are less plausible but can deliver more precise estimates. The staggered no-anticipation assumption (Assumption 5) is Yi,t(g)=Yi,t(∞)Y_{i,t}(g)=Y_{i,t}(\infty)Yi,t​(g)=Yi,t​(∞) for all iii and t<gt<gt<g: while a unit is untreated, its outcome does not depend on its future treatment date.

Static and Dynamic TWFE under Staggered Timing

In the two-period model the population coefficient of the TWFE regression is the ATT. The question is whether its usual multi-period generalizations keep a causal interpretation. The static specification is:

Yi,t=αi+ϕt+Di,tβpost+ϵi,t(9)Y_{i,t}=\alpha_i+\phi_t+D_{i,t}\beta_{post}+\epsilon_{i,t} \tag{9}Yi,t​=αi​+ϕt​+Di,t​βpost​+ϵi,t​(9)

Let τi,t(g)=Yi,t(g)−Yi,t(∞)\tau_{i,t}(g)=Y_{i,t}(g)-Y_{i,t}(\infty)τi,t​(g)=Yi,t​(g)−Yi,t​(∞). If τi,t(g)=τ\tau_{i,t}(g)=\tauτi,t​(g)=τ for all units whenever t≥gt\geq gt≥g, then under Assumptions 4 and 5 βpost=τ\beta_{post}=\tauβpost​=τ. If effects vary only with time since treatment, τi,t(g)=∑s≥0τs1[t−g=s]\tau_{i,t}(g)=\sum_{s\geq0}\tau_s1[t-g=s]τi,t​(g)=∑s≥0​τs​1[t−g=s], then βpost=∑sωsτs\beta_{post}=\sum_s\omega_s\tau_sβpost​=∑s​ωs​τs​, where the weights ωs\omega_sωs​ sum to one but may be negative. All τs\tau_sτs​ can then be positive while βpost\beta_{post}βpost​ is negative, and long-run effects are the ones that typically receive negative weight. With heterogeneity across both units and time, τi,t(g)\tau_{i,t}(g)τi,t​(g) can get negative weight for some combinations of ttt and ggg. The decomposition of Goodman-Bacon (2021) gives the intuition: β^post\widehat{\beta}_{post}β​post​ is a convex weighted average of two-group, two-period DiD comparisons in which one group changes treatment status and the other does not, and some of these comparisons use an earlier-treated group as the control for a later-treated group. A unit treated early receives negative weight if it serves as a control for many later-treated units.

The algebra behind the negative weights uses the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem. Let D^i,t\widehat{D}_{i,t}Di,t​ be the fitted value from the regression Di,t=α~i+ϕ~t+ui,tD_{i,t}=\tilde{\alpha}_i+\tilde{\phi}_t+u_{i,t}Di,t​=α~i​+ϕ~​t​+ui,t​. Then:

β^post=∑i,t(Di,t−D^i,t)Yi,t∑i,t(Di,t−D^i,t)2(10)\widehat{\beta}_{post}=\frac{\sum_{i,t}\left(D_{i,t}-\widehat{D}_{i,t}\right)Y_{i,t}}{\sum_{i,t}\left(D_{i,t}-\widehat{D}_{i,t}\right)^2} \tag{10}β​post​=∑i,t​(Di,t​−Di,t​)2∑i,t​(Di,t​−Di,t​)Yi,t​​(10)

If Di,t=1D_{i,t}=1Di,t​=1 and D^i,t>1\widehat{D}_{i,t}>1Di,t​>1, the estimator is decreasing in Yi,tY_{i,t}Yi,t​ although the observation is treated, and since Yi,t=Yi,t(∞)+τi,t(g)Y_{i,t}=Y_{i,t}(\infty)+\tau_{i,t}(g)Yi,t​=Yi,t​(∞)+τi,t​(g) the effect τi,t(g)\tau_{i,t}(g)τi,t​(g) gets negative weight. In a balanced panel the fitted value is:

D^i,t=D‾i+D‾t−D‾,D‾i=T−1∑tDi,t,D‾t=N−1∑iDi,t,D‾=(NT)−1∑i,tDi,t(11)\widehat{D}_{i,t}=\overline{D}_i+\overline{D}_t-\overline{D},\qquad\overline{D}_i=T^{-1}\sum_tD_{i,t},\quad\overline{D}_t=N^{-1}\sum_iD_{i,t},\quad\overline{D}=(NT)^{-1}\sum_{i,t}D_{i,t} \tag{11}Di,t​=Di​+Dt​−D,Di​=T−1t∑​Di,t​,Dt​=N−1i∑​Di,t​,D=(NT)−1i,t∑​Di,t​(11)

Negative weights therefore fall on early adopters in late periods. When effects are homogeneous, the negative weights on τ\tauτ cancel against positive weights and βpost\beta_{post}βpost​ recovers τ\tauτ.

The dynamic specification (event-study regression) replaces the treatment indicator by indicators for time relative to treatment:

Yi,t=αi+ϕt+∑r≠01[Ri,t=r]βr+ϵi,t(12)Y_{i,t}=\alpha_i+\phi_t+\sum_{r\neq0}1[R_{i,t}=r]\beta_r+\epsilon_{i,t} \tag{12}Yi,t​=αi​+ϕt​+r=0∑​1[Ri,t​=r]βr​+ϵi,t​(12)

where Ri,t=t−Gi+1R_{i,t}=t-G_i+1Ri,t​=t−Gi​+1, so that Ri,t=1R_{i,t}=1Ri,t​=1 in the first treated period and the omitted category r=0r=0r=0 is the last period before treatment. If effects vary only with time since treatment, so that all cohorts have effect τs\tau_sτs​ in the period with t−g=st-g=st−g=s, the specification recovers the dynamic effects under Assumptions 4 and 5: βs+1=τs\beta_{s+1}=\tau_sβs+1​=τs​. The paper prints this as βs=τs\beta_s=\tau_sβs​=τs​, which does not match its own definition of Ri,tR_{i,t}Ri,t​. It suffices that the cohort-average effect at each horizon is the same for all cohorts, and all relative-time indicators must be included (binning endpoints can cause problems). When dynamic effects differ across cohorts, Sun and Abraham (2021) show two failures. First, βr\beta_rβr​ can put negative weight on the effect rrr periods after treatment for some units. Second, βr\beta_rβr​ can put non-zero weight on effects at other lags r′≠rr'\neq rr′=r, a cross-lag contamination. Hence the lead coefficients need not be zero even if parallel trends holds in every period (and conversely), so pre-trends judged from this regression can be misleading. Diagnostics for the static specification report the number of group-time effects with negative weights and the amount of heterogeneity needed to reverse the sign (de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille 2020), the weights on each two-by-two comparison (Goodman-Bacon 2021), or tests of the constant-effect assumption (Jakiela 2021).

Heterogeneity-Robust Estimators

The new estimators follow the logic of the canonical model: define a causal parameter, use parallel trends and no anticipation to impute the counterfactual from a clean control group, and replace expectations by sample means. Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021, CS) use as building block the group-time average treatment effect, the average effect at time ttt for the cohort first treated in ggg. Under Assumption 4.a (and no anticipation, Assumption 5), for t≥gt\geq gt≥g and any cohort g′>tg'>tg′>t:

ATT(g,t)=E[Yi,t(g)−Yi,t(∞)∣Gi=g]=E[Yi,t−Yi,g−1∣Gi=g]−E[Yi,t−Yi,g−1∣Gi=g′](13)\begin{aligned} ATT(g,t)&=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,t}(g)-Y_{i,t}(\infty)\mid G_i=g\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,t}-Y_{i,g-1}\mid G_i=g\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,t}-Y_{i,g-1}\mid G_i=g'\right] \end{aligned} \tag{13}ATT(g,t)​=E[Yi,t​(g)−Yi,t​(∞)∣Gi​=g]=E[Yi,t​−Yi,g−1​∣Gi​=g]−E[Yi,t​−Yi,g−1​∣Gi​=g′]​(13)

This is the multi-period analog of the canonical result: cohort ggg is untreated in period g−1g-1g−1, cohort g′g'g′ is untreated in both g−1g-1g−1 and ttt, and parallel trends between these two periods links them. The equality also holds when the comparison is averaged over any set Gcomp\mathcal{G}_{comp}Gcomp​ of cohorts with g′>tg'>tg′>t for all g′∈Gcompg'\in\mathcal{G}_{comp}g′∈Gcomp​, which gives the estimator:

ATT^(g,t)=1Ng∑i:Gi=g[Yi,t−Yi,g−1]−1NGcomp∑i:Gi∈Gcomp[Yi,t−Yi,g−1](14)\widehat{ATT}(g,t)=\frac{1}{N_g}\sum_{i:G_i=g}\left[Y_{i,t}-Y_{i,g-1}\right]-\frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{G}_{comp}}}\sum_{i:G_i\in\mathcal{G}_{comp}}\left[Y_{i,t}-Y_{i,g-1}\right] \tag{14}ATT(g,t)=Ng​1​i:Gi​=g∑​[Yi,t​−Yi,g−1​]−NGcomp​​1​i:Gi​∈Gcomp​∑​[Yi,t​−Yi,g−1​](14)

where NgN_gNg​ and NGcompN_{\mathcal{G}_{comp}}NGcomp​​ are the numbers of units in cohort ggg and in the comparison set. CS consider two comparison sets: the never-treated units, Gcomp={∞}\mathcal{G}_{comp}=\{\infty\}Gcomp​={∞}, and all not-yet-treated units, Gcomp={g′:g′>t}\mathcal{G}_{comp}=\{g':g'>t\}Gcomp​={g′:g′>t}. If the never-treated are not in the comparison set, a version of Assumption 4.a that excludes them suffices. The group-time effects can be aggregated into any weighted average, for example the event-study parameter for the effect lll periods after adoption:

ATTlw=∑gwgATT(g,g+l)(15)ATT^w_l=\sum_gw_gATT(g,g+l) \tag{15}ATTlw​=g∑​wg​ATT(g,g+l)(15)

where the weights wgw_gwg​ may weight cohorts equally or by their frequency in the treated population. Inference uses the delta method or a bootstrap. Two advantages over TWFE follow: the estimand is sensible under arbitrary heterogeneity (no negative weights, and weights chosen by the researcher instead of by the variance of the treatment indicator), and the control group is transparent.

Imputation estimators (Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess 2021, BJS; also Gardner 2021, Liu et al. 2022, Wooldridge 2021) fit the TWFE model Yi,t(∞)=αi+λt+ϵi,tY_{i,t}(\infty)=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\epsilon_{i,t}Yi,t​(∞)=αi​+λt​+ϵi,t​ on not-yet-treated observations only, predict Y^i,t(∞)\widehat{Y}_{i,t}(\infty)Yi,t​(∞) for treated observations, and aggregate the unit-level estimates Yi,t−Y^i,t(∞)Y_{i,t}-\widehat{Y}_{i,t}(\infty)Yi,t​−Yi,t​(∞) into summary parameters. They are valid under Assumptions 4 and 5. The difference from CS is clearest with three periods and G={3,∞}\mathcal{G}=\{3,\infty\}G={3,∞}. Writing Yˉt,g\bar{Y}_{t,g}Yˉt,g​ for the mean outcome in period ttt of units with Gi=gG_i=gGi​=g and Yˉpre,g=12(Yˉ1,g+Yˉ2,g)\bar{Y}_{pre,g}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\bar{Y}_{1,g}+\bar{Y}_{2,g}\right)Yˉpre,g​=21​(Yˉ1,g​+Yˉ2,g​):

ATT^(3,3)=(Yˉ3,3−Yˉ3,∞)−(Yˉ2,3−Yˉ2,∞)ATT^BJS(3,3)=(Yˉ3,3−Yˉ3,∞)−(Yˉpre,3−Yˉpre,∞)(16)\begin{aligned} \widehat{ATT}(3,3)&=\left(\bar{Y}_{3,3}-\bar{Y}_{3,\infty}\right)-\left(\bar{Y}_{2,3}-\bar{Y}_{2,\infty}\right)\\ \widehat{ATT}_{BJS}(3,3)&=\left(\bar{Y}_{3,3}-\bar{Y}_{3,\infty}\right)-\left(\bar{Y}_{pre,3}-\bar{Y}_{pre,\infty}\right) \end{aligned} \tag{16}ATT(3,3)ATTBJS​(3,3)​=(Yˉ3,3​−Yˉ3,∞​)−(Yˉ2,3​−Yˉ2,∞​)=(Yˉ3,3​−Yˉ3,∞​)−(Yˉpre,3​−Yˉpre,∞​)​(16)

CS compare with the last pre-treatment period, BJS with the average of all pre-treatment periods. Averaging raises precision: BJS show their estimator is efficient under Assumption 4 with homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated errors, whereas if Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​(0) follows a random walk the earlier periods carry no extra information and ignoring them is efficient. The price is a stronger identifying assumption, parallel trends over all periods (Assumption 4) instead of post-treatment parallel trends only (Assumption 4.a), and a larger bias when trends diverge gradually, because comparisons span periods farther apart. BJS adjust for covariates linearly, CS more generally.

Other estimators differ in the control group and the weights. The estimator of de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020) corresponds in the staggered case to the CS estimator of ATT0wATT^w_0ATT0w​ with particular weights. Sun and Abraham (2021) use the form of ATT^(g,t)\widehat{ATT}(g,t)ATT(g,t) with the never-treated or, if there are none, the last-treated cohort as comparison, Gcomp={max⁡iGi}\mathcal{G}_{comp}=\{\max_iG_i\}Gcomp​={maxi​Gi​}. Marcus and Sant'Anna (2021) propose a recursive estimator that exploits the CS assumptions more efficiently. Stacked regressions (Cengiz et al. 2019) match each treatment event to clean controls with event-specific fixed effects; Gardner (2021) shows they estimate a convex weighted average of the ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t), with weights set by the number of treated units and the variance of treatment within each event. When treatment can turn on and off, estimators compare units whose status changes with units whose status is constant over the same periods; they need a no carryover assumption (potential outcomes depend only on current treatment), or else a stronger parallel trends assumption that holds regardless of the treatment path. Further work covers fuzzy designs, where the share of treated units rises in one group but not in the other, and multi-valued or continuous treatments.

Conditional Parallel Trends

Parallel trends can fail because of time-varying confounders and because it depends on functional form: if it holds for Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​(0) in levels it generally fails for log⁡(Yi,t(0))\log(Y_{i,t}(0))log(Yi,t​(0)). Roth and Sant'Anna (2023) show that it holds for all monotonic transformations essentially only if the population splits into one group that is as good as randomly assigned and one group whose potential outcome distribution is the same in both periods. One way to make the assumption more credible is to impose it conditional on a vector XiX_iXi​ of pre-treatment covariates (Assumption 6, conditional parallel trends), almost surely:

E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=1,Xi]=E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=0,Xi](17)\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=1,X_i\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=0,X_i\right] \tag{17}E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=1,Xi​]=E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=0,Xi​](17)

Strong overlap (Assumption 7) requires that for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, P(Di=1∣Xi)<1−ϵP(D_i=1\mid X_i)<1-\epsilonP(Di​=1∣Xi​)<1−ϵ almost surely and E[D]>0\mathbb{E}[D]>0E[D]>0, so that every treated unit has untreated counterparts with the same covariates. Under Assumptions 2, 6 and 7 the conditional effect τ2(x)=E[Yi,2(1)−Yi,2(0)∣Di=1,Xi=x]\tau_2(x)=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(1)-Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1,X_i=x\right]τ2​(x)=E[Yi,2​(1)−Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1,Xi​=x] is identified by the canonical argument applied within the cell Xi=xX_i=xXi​=x:

τ2(x)=E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=1,Xi=x]−E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0,Xi=x](18)\tau_2(x)=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1,X_i=x\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0,X_i=x\right] \tag{18}τ2​(x)=E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=1,Xi​=x]−E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0,Xi​=x](18)

and by the law of iterated expectations τ2=E[τ2(Xi)∣Di=1]\tau_2=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_2(X_i)\mid D_i=1\right]τ2​=E[τ2​(Xi​)∣Di​=1]. With a discrete XiX_iXi​ taking few values one runs a DiD in each cell and averages. Otherwise it is tempting to add a time-by-covariate interaction to the TWFE regression:

Yi,t=αi+ϕt+(1[t=2]⋅Di)β+(Xi⋅1[t=2])γ+εi,t(19)Y_{i,t}=\alpha_i+\phi_t+\left(1[t=2]\cdot D_i\right)\beta+\left(X_i\cdot1[t=2]\right)\gamma+\varepsilon_{i,t} \tag{19}Yi,t​=αi​+ϕt​+(1[t=2]⋅Di​)β+(Xi​⋅1[t=2])γ+εi,t​(19)

This need not be consistent for the ATT without additional homogeneity assumptions. It models the conditional expectation of Yi,2−Yi,1Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}Yi,2​−Yi,1​ as linear in XiX_iXi​ with the same slope γ\gammaγ for both groups, whereas with treatment effects that vary with XiX_iXi​ the slope differs by treatment status. Three alternatives are available. Regression adjustment (Heckman, Ichimura and Todd 1997) rests on:

τ2=E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=1]−E[E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0,Xi]∣Di=1](20)\tau_2=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0,X_i\right]\mid D_i=1\right] \tag{20}τ2​=E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=1]−E[E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0,Xi​]∣Di​=1](20)

so one estimates the conditional mean of the outcome change among untreated units and averages its predictions over the covariates of the treated units:

τ^2=1N1∑i:Di=1((Yi,2−Yi,1)−E^[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0,Xi])(21)\widehat{\tau}_2=\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:D_i=1}\left(\left(Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\right)-\widehat{\mathbb{E}}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0,X_i\right]\right) \tag{21}τ2​=N1​1​i:Di​=1∑​((Yi,2​−Yi,1​)−E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0,Xi​])(21)

Nearest-neighbour matching is a special case in which the prediction is the outcome change of the matched untreated unit l(i)l(i)l(i); with a fixed number of matches the estimator is not asymptotically linear and the standard bootstrap is invalid. and is consistent if the propensity score model is correctly specified. The doubly robust estimand of Sant'Anna and Zhao (2020) combines the two:

τ2=E[(DiE[Di]−(1−Di)p(Xi)1−p(Xi)E[(1−Di)p(Xi)1−p(Xi)])(Yi,2−Yi,1−E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0,Xi])](23)\tau_2=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{D_i}{\mathbb{E}\left[D_i\right]}-\frac{\frac{(1-D_i)p(X_i)}{1-p(X_i)}}{\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-D_i)p(X_i)}{1-p(X_i)}\right]}\right)\left(Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0,X_i\right]\right)\right] \tag{23}τ2​=E​​E[Di​]Di​​−E[1−p(Xi​)(1−Di​)p(Xi​)​]1−p(Xi​)(1−Di​)p(Xi​)​​​(Yi,2​−Yi,1​−E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0,Xi​])​(23)

Its plug-in estimator is consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity score model is correct, attains the semiparametric efficiency bound when both are, and can be combined with machine-learning first steps. CS extend all three procedures to ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t); Wooldridge (2021) proposes a regression adjustment for staggered designs that uses more pre-treatment periods, with more precision and more bias if the extra assumptions fail.

Two caveats apply. Covariates must not be affected by the treatment, otherwise conditioning on them creates a bad control problem; an exogenous time-varying covariate Wi,tW_{i,t}Wi,t​ can be included through its whole path Wi=(Wi,1,…,Wi,T)′W_i=(W_{i,1},\dots,W_{i,T})'Wi​=(Wi,1​,…,Wi,T​)′. And if the lagged outcome is part of XiX_iXi​, the Yi,1(0)Y_{i,1}(0)Yi,1​(0) terms cancel and conditional parallel trends reduces to conditional mean independence of the untreated potential outcome:

E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=1,Xi]=E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=0,Xi](24)\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1,X_i\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=0,X_i\right] \tag{24}E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1,Xi​]=E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=0,Xi​](24)

Conditioning on lagged outcomes is sensible when treatment is as good as random given them, but it can raise bias through mean reversion when groups differ in levels and share the same trend. Unconfoundedness given the lagged outcome and parallel trends are non-nested assumptions.

Testing for Pre-Trends

Add a period t=0t=0t=0 in which no unit is treated to the canonical model. By no anticipation, Yi,t=Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}=Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​=Yi,t​(0) for all units in t=0t=0t=0 and t=1t=1t=1, so the analog of parallel trends between these periods is testable. In the event-study regression above (valid here because timing is not staggered), the lead coefficient is:

β^−1=1N1∑i:Di=1(Yi,0−Yi,1)−1N0∑i:Di=0(Yi,0−Yi,1)(25)\widehat{\beta}_{-1}=\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:D_i=1}\left(Y_{i,0}-Y_{i,1}\right)-\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i:D_i=0}\left(Y_{i,0}-Y_{i,1}\right) \tag{25}β​−1​=N1​1​i:Di​=1∑​(Yi,0​−Yi,1​)−N0​1​i:Di​=0∑​(Yi,0​−Yi,1​)(25)

where N0N_0N0​ is the number of untreated units (the paper prints the summands without parentheses). The pre-trends test is the test of β−1=0\beta_{-1}=0β−1​=0, and with several pre-treatment periods the β^r\widehat{\beta}_rβ​r​ are shown in an event-study plot. With staggered timing or covariates the plot should use placebo estimates of ATTlwATT^w_lATTlw​ for l<0l<0l<0 from a heterogeneity-robust estimator, not the dynamic TWFE regression. The paper lists four problems. First, parallel pre-trends do not guarantee parallel post-treatment trends. Second, the test has low power. Suppose there is no treatment effect and a linear difference in trends. Then ∣β−1∣=∣β1∣|\beta_{-1}|=|\beta_1|∣β−1​∣=∣β1​∣, and if β^−1\widehat{\beta}_{-1}β​−1​ and β^1\widehat{\beta}_1β​1​ have the same sampling variance, they are significant with the same probability. A linear violation that the pre-test detects only half of the time therefore produces a spurious significant effect half of the time, ten times the rate expected from a nominal 95 percent confidence interval. The pre-test takes parallel trends as the null, so it controls the probability of finding a violation when there is none and not the probability of missing one. Third, conditioning on passing the pre-test selects draws of the data and creates pre-test bias, which in many cases adds to the bias from the violation itself (Roth 2022). Fourth, the conventional approach gives no guidance once a significant pre-trend is found, although a small violation need not prevent learning about the effect.

Improved diagnostics include the power calculations of Roth (2022) against violations specified by the researcher, and non-inferiority tests that reverse the hypotheses. Dette and Schumann (2020) test H0:max⁡r<0∣βr∣≥cH_0:\max_{r<0}|\beta_r|\geq cH0​:maxr<0​∣βr​∣≥c, so the test detects a pre-trend of magnitude at least ccc with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha1−α. These tests are powered against large violations by design, but they give no guarantee for the confidence interval of the treatment effect and do not remove pre-testing problems.

Robust Inference and Sensitivity Analysis

Rambachan and Roth (2022b) formalize the idea behind pre-trend testing, that counterfactual post-treatment trends cannot be too different from pre-trends. In the three-period, non-staggered setting, the post-treatment violation of parallel trends and its pre-treatment analog are:

δ1=E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=1]−E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=0]δ−1=E[Yi,0(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=1]−E[Yi,0(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=0](26)\begin{aligned} \delta_1&=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=0\right]\\ \delta_{-1}&=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,0}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,0}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=0\right] \end{aligned} \tag{26}δ1​δ−1​​=E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=0]=E[Yi,0​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,0​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=0]​(26)

The bias δ1\delta_1δ1​ is not identified, while δ−1=E[β^−1]\delta_{-1}=\mathbb{E}\left[\widehat{\beta}_{-1}\right]δ−1​=E[β​−1​] is. Inference is carried out under restrictions on δ1\delta_1δ1​ given δ−1\delta_{-1}δ−1​, or given δ−1,…,δ−K\delta_{-1},\dots,\delta_{-K}δ−1​,…,δ−K​ with KKK pre-treatment coefficients. The relative magnitudes restriction is:

∣δ1∣≤Mˉmax⁡r<0∣δr∣(27)|\delta_1|\leq\bar{M}\max_{r<0}|\delta_r| \tag{27}∣δ1​∣≤Mˉr<0max​∣δr​∣(27)

so that with Mˉ=1\bar{M}=1Mˉ=1 the post-treatment violation is no larger than the largest pre-treatment violation. A second family, smoothness restrictions, bounds how far δ1\delta_1δ1​ can deviate from a linear extrapolation of the pre-treatment differences in trends. Tools from the partial identification literature give confidence sets for the ATT that are uniformly valid under the restriction and that account for the fact that only an estimate β^−1\widehat{\beta}_{-1}β​−1​ of δ−1\delta_{-1}δ−1​ is observed. These sets widen when the pre-treatment coefficients are imprecise, whereas a conventional pre-test becomes less likely to reject. The natural summary is the breakdown value: a positive effect that is robust up to Mˉ=2\bar{M}=2Mˉ=2 can be overturned only by a post-treatment violation twice the largest pre-treatment one. The method applies whenever there is an effect estimate β^post\widehat{\beta}_{post}β​post​ and a placebo estimate β^pre\widehat{\beta}_{pre}β​pre​ and the bias of the first can be bounded given the expectation of the second, including staggered designs and conditional parallel trends.

Ye et al. (2021) bound the ATT with two control groups, Ci=aC_i=aCi​=a and Ci=bC_i=bCi​=b, whose trends bracket that of the treated group Ci=trtC_i=trtCi​=trt. With Δ(c)=E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Ci=c]\Delta(c)=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid C_i=c\right]Δ(c)=E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Ci​=c], the assumption and, together with no anticipation, the implied bounds are:

min⁡{Δ(a),Δ(b)}≤Δ(trt)≤max⁡{Δ(a),Δ(b)}E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=1]−max⁡{Δ(a),Δ(b)}≤τ2≤E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=1]−min⁡{Δ(a),Δ(b)}(28)\begin{aligned} &\min\{\Delta(a),\Delta(b)\}\leq\Delta(trt)\leq\max\{\Delta(a),\Delta(b)\}\\ &\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1\right]-\max\{\Delta(a),\Delta(b)\}\leq\tau_2\leq\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1\right]-\min\{\Delta(a),\Delta(b)\} \end{aligned} \tag{28}​min{Δ(a),Δ(b)}≤Δ(trt)≤max{Δ(a),Δ(b)}E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=1]−max{Δ(a),Δ(b)}≤τ2​≤E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=1]−min{Δ(a),Δ(b)}​(28)

An example is a treated set of industries with one control group that is more cyclical and one that is less cyclical. Other approaches summarize the strength of confounding needed to produce a given bias (Keele et al. 2019), plot the smoothest trend through the event-study plot that is consistent with no effect (Freyaldenhoven et al. 2021), or use a covariate affected by the confounds but not by the treatment (Freyaldenhoven et al. 2019).

Inference with Few Clusters

Cluster-robust inference relies on a central limit theorem in the number of treated and untreated clusters. With few clusters it can fail even when each cluster is large, because cluster-level shocks do not average out within a cluster. Model-based approaches start from a structural equation for unit iii in cluster jjj and its cluster average:

Yijt=αj+ϕt+Djtβ+(νjt+ϵijt)Yjt=αj+ϕt+Djtβ+ηjt,ηjt=νjt+nj−1∑i=1njϵijt(29)\begin{aligned} Y_{ijt}&=\alpha_j+\phi_t+D_{jt}\beta+\left(\nu_{jt}+\epsilon_{ijt}\right)\\ Y_{jt}&=\alpha_j+\phi_t+D_{jt}\beta+\eta_{jt},\qquad\eta_{jt}=\nu_{jt}+n_j^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\epsilon_{ijt} \end{aligned} \tag{29}Yijt​Yjt​​=αj​+ϕt​+Djt​β+(νjt​+ϵijt​)=αj​+ϕt​+Djt​β+ηjt​,ηjt​=νjt​+nj−1​i=1∑nj​​ϵijt​​(29)

where DjtD_{jt}Djt​ indicates that cluster jjj is treated in period ttt, νjt\nu_{jt}νjt​ is a common cluster-by-time error, ϵijt\epsilon_{ijt}ϵijt​ is an idiosyncratic error and njn_jnj​ is the number of units in cluster jjj. With two periods and treatment DjD_jDj​ starting in period 2, the cluster-level DiD estimator is:

β^=β+1J1∑j:Dj=1(Δνj+nj−1∑i=1njΔϵij)−1J0∑j:Dj=0(Δνj+nj−1∑i=1njΔϵij)(30)\widehat{\beta}=\beta+\frac{1}{J_1}\sum_{j:D_j=1}\left(\Delta\nu_j+n_j^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\Delta\epsilon_{ij}\right)-\frac{1}{J_0}\sum_{j:D_j=0}\left(\Delta\nu_j+n_j^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\Delta\epsilon_{ij}\right) \tag{30}β​=β+J1​1​j:Dj​=1∑​(Δνj​+nj−1​i=1∑nj​​Δϵij​)−J0​1​j:Dj​=0∑​(Δνj​+nj−1​i=1∑nj​​Δϵij​)(30)

where JdJ_dJd​ is the number of clusters with treatment ddd and Δνj=νj2−νj1\Delta\nu_j=\nu_{j2}-\nu_{j1}Δνj​=νj2​−νj1​ (likewise for the other variables). With few clusters the averages of Δνj\Delta\nu_jΔνj​ are not approximately normal and their variance is hard to estimate. The appendix links this model to potential outcomes: under Assumptions 1 and 2 at the cluster level the estimator takes this form with β=τ2\beta=\tau_2β=τ2​, νjt=νjt,0+Djνjt,1\nu_{jt}=\nu_{jt,0}+D_j\nu_{jt,1}νjt​=νjt,0​+Dj​νjt,1​ and ϵijt=ϵijt,0+Djϵijt,1\epsilon_{ijt}=\epsilon_{ijt,0}+D_j\epsilon_{ijt,1}ϵijt​=ϵijt,0​+Dj​ϵijt,1​, where:

ϵijt,0=Yijt(0)−E[Yijt(0)∣j(i)=j]ϵijt,1=Yijt(1)−Yijt(0)−E[Yijt(1)−Yijt(0)∣j(i)=j]νjt,0=E[Yijt(0)∣j(i)=j]−E[Yijt(0)∣Dj]νjt,1=E[Yijt(1)−Yijt(0)∣j(i)=j]−τt(31)\begin{aligned} \epsilon_{ijt,0}&=Y_{ijt}(0)-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{ijt}(0)\mid j(i)=j\right]\\ \epsilon_{ijt,1}&=Y_{ijt}(1)-Y_{ijt}(0)-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{ijt}(1)-Y_{ijt}(0)\mid j(i)=j\right]\\ \nu_{jt,0}&=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{ijt}(0)\mid j(i)=j\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{ijt}(0)\mid D_j\right]\\ \nu_{jt,1}&=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{ijt}(1)-Y_{ijt}(0)\mid j(i)=j\right]-\tau_t \end{aligned} \tag{31}ϵijt,0​ϵijt,1​νjt,0​νjt,1​​=Yijt​(0)−E[Yijt​(0)∣j(i)=j]=Yijt​(1)−Yijt​(0)−E[Yijt​(1)−Yijt​(0)∣j(i)=j]=E[Yijt​(0)∣j(i)=j]−E[Yijt​(0)∣Dj​]=E[Yijt​(1)−Yijt​(0)∣j(i)=j]−τt​​(31)

and j(i)j(i)j(i) is the cluster of unit iii. Restrictions on the errors are thus restrictions on cluster-level heterogeneity in untreated outcomes and in treatment effects. The methods differ in which homogeneity they impose:

  • Donald and Lang (2007): νjt\nu_{jt}νjt​ is mean-zero Gaussian, homoskedastic across clusters and treatment status, and nj→∞n_j\rightarrow\inftynj​→∞; inference uses a ttt distribution with J−2J-2J−2 degrees of freedom, where JJJ is the total number of clusters. It is valid with few treated and few untreated clusters but rests on a strong parametric assumption.

  • Conley and Taber (2011): with J0J_0J0​ large and J1J_1J1​ small, the distribution of errors is learned from the control clusters under the assumption that treated clusters share it; no Gaussianity is needed, but heterogeneous treatment effects or cluster sizes violate the assumption. Ferman and Pinto (2019) allow heteroskedasticity from cluster size or other observables.

  • Hagemann (2020): a permutation approach whose type I error is bounded given a bound on relative heterogeneity across clusters; it rules out cluster-specific heterogeneity in trends of untreated potential outcomes.

  • Cluster wild bootstrap: simulations of Cameron, Gelbach and Miller (2008) suggest it can work with as few as five clusters, but Canay, Santos and Shaikh (2021) show its validity with few large clusters requires homogeneity conditions on treatment effects that TWFE regressions with cluster and time fixed effects commonly violate; it can perform poorly with few treated clusters.

  • Many periods: permutation, ttt-test based and conformal procedures relax these conditions when TTT is large, at the cost of limiting the serial dependence of cluster shocks and assuming parallel trends over many periods.

  • Conditioning on the shocks: treat νjt\nu_{jt}νjt​ as fixed, cluster at the unit level, and regard cluster-level shocks as a violation of parallel trends to be handled by the sensitivity analysis above.

  • Fisher randomization tests: recompute a test statistic under permutations of treatment across clusters. If treatment is randomly assigned the test is exact in finite samples under the sharp null of no effect for any unit, with no restriction on potential outcomes; random assignment is often questionable in DiD, and the sharp null is less interesting than the null of no average effect.

Design-Based Inference and the Level of Clustering

The sampling view raises two conceptual difficulties: the super-population may be hard to imagine (the 50 US states), and the correct level of clustering is unclear. A design-based framework treats the units and their potential outcomes as fixed and the treatment assignment as the source of randomness. Rambachan and Roth (2022a) extend it to DiD, where treatment probabilities differ across units in unknown ways. Let πi\pi_iπi​ be the probability that Di=1D_i=1Di​=1. The finite-population version of parallel trends is that treatment probabilities are uncorrelated with trends in Y(0)Y(0)Y(0):

∑i=1N(πi−N1N)(Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0))=0(32)\sum_{i=1}^N\left(\pi_i-\frac{N_1}{N}\right)\left(Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\right)=0 \tag{32}i=1∑N​(πi​−NN1​​)(Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0))=0(32)

Under this condition the usual DiD estimator is unbiased for a finite-population analog of the ATT, ED[τ^2]=τ2FinE_D\left[\widehat{\tau}_2\right]=\tau^{Fin}_2ED​[τ2​]=τ2Fin​, where the expectation EDE_DED​ is over the assignment of treatment:

τ2Fin=ED[1N1∑i:Di=1(Yi,2(1)−Yi,2(0))](33)\tau^{Fin}_2=E_D\left[\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:D_i=1}\left(Y_{i,2}(1)-Y_{i,2}(0)\right)\right] \tag{33}τ2Fin​=ED​[N1​1​i:Di​=1∑​(Yi,2​(1)−Yi,2​(0))](33)

Cluster-robust standard errors are valid, though possibly conservative, when clustering is at the level at which treatment is independently determined: the unit if treatment is assigned independently across units, the state if it is determined independently across states. This contrasts with the model-based rule of clustering at the level at which errors are correlated. The usual methods thus remain valid without a super-population.

Other Topics

Section 6 of the paper lists further directions. For distributional effects, the changes-in-changes model of Athey and Imbens (2006) recovers the full counterfactual distribution of Y(0)Y(0)Y(0) for the treated group by assuming that the mapping between quantiles of the two groups is stable over time; alternatives assume parallel trends for the log characteristic function (Bonhomme and Sauder 2011) or copula stability (Callaway and Li 2019), and Roth and Sant'Anna (2023) show that parallel trends holds for all functional forms under a parallel-trends-type condition on the cumulative distribution of Y(0)Y(0)Y(0). If treatment timing is as good as random, more efficient estimators than staggered DiD exist (Roth and Sant'Anna 2021). When treatment turns on and off, sequential ignorability from biostatistics is an alternative to parallel trends, preferable when lagged outcomes feed back into treatment. Spillovers violate SUTVA and are handled in extensions such as Butts (2021). Triple differences compare the DiD for an affected demographic group with the DiD for an unaffected one, and can often be cast as a DiD on a transformed outcome Y~\tilde{Y}Y~ equal to the difference in outcomes between the two groups. Links to synthetic control and to machine-learning estimation of conditional effects are open areas.

Recommendations and Software

The paper's checklist for practitioners (its Table 1) asks three questions.

  • Is everyone treated at the same time? If yes and the panel is balanced, static or dynamic TWFE specifications give easily interpretable estimates. If no, use a heterogeneity-robust estimator, chosen according to whether treatment turns on and off and which parallel trends assumption is acceptable; use TWFE only if treatment effect heterogeneity can be restricted. The robust estimators typically, though not always, give similar answers, so the first-order concern is a clear target parameter and comparison group.

  • Is parallel trends surely valid? If yes, explain why, including the choice of functional form; if the reason is quasi-random timing, consider a more efficient estimator. If no: condition on covariates when that makes parallel trends more plausible, with doubly robust methods as the default and regression adjustment under limited overlap; draw an event-study plot (from the dynamic TWFE regression with a common treatment date, from robust estimators otherwise), with simultaneous confidence bands; report the power of the pre-test against relevant alternatives or non-inferiority tests; and report formal sensitivity analyses such as the breakdown value of Mˉ\bar{M}Mˉ, interpreted with context-specific knowledge of likely confounds.

  • Is there a large number of treated and untreated clusters sampled from a super-population? If yes, use cluster-robust methods, clustering at the level at which treatment is independently assigned. With few treated clusters, use one of the alternative methods whose homogeneity assumption fits the context. If no super-population is conceivable, rely on the design-based justification.

The paper's Table 2 lists R and Stata packages.

  • Heterogeneity-robust estimators: did and csdid (Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021); did2s (Gardner 2021 and several others); didimputation and did_imputation (Borusyak et al. 2021); DIDmultiplegt and did_multiplegt (de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille 2020); eventstudyinteract and fixest (Sun and Abraham 2021); flexpaneldid (Dettmann 2020); stackedev (stacking as in Cengiz et al. 2019); staggered (Roth and Sant'Anna 2021, also Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021 and Sun and Abraham 2021); xtevent (Freyaldenhoven et al. 2019).

  • Covariates: DRDID and drdid (Sant'Anna and Zhao 2020).

  • TWFE diagnostics: bacondecomp and ddtiming (Goodman-Bacon 2021); TwoWayFEWeights (de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille 2020).

  • Violations of parallel trends: honestDiD (Rambachan and Roth 2022b); pretrends (Roth 2022).

References

  • Roth, Jonathan, Pedro HC Sant'Anna, Alyssa Bilinski, and John Poe. 2023. “What's Trending in Difference-in-Differences? A Synthesis of the Recent Econometrics Literature.” Journal of Econometrics, 235(2): 2218–2244.

This equation defines the target parameter of the canonical two-period model, the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) in period 2. Yi,2(1)Y_{i,2}(1)Yi,2​(1) is the period-2 outcome of unit iii along the path "treated from period 2 on" and Yi,2(0)Y_{i,2}(0)Yi,2​(0) is its period-2 outcome along the path "never treated"; their difference is the unit-level causal effect, measured in the units of the outcome and of either sign. The expectation is taken over the treated population only (Di=1D_i=1Di​=1), so τ2\tau_2τ2​ says nothing about what the treatment would do to the comparison population.

Because treated units are observed under treatment, Yi,2=Yi,2(1)Y_{i,2}=Y_{i,2}(1)Yi,2​=Yi,2​(1) for them and the first half of the ATT is a population mean of observables. The second half is a counterfactual:

τ2=E[Yi,2∣Di=1]⏟observed−E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=1]⏟never observed\tau_2=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}\mid D_i=1\right]}_{\text{observed}}-\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]}_{\text{never observed}}τ2​=observedE[Yi,2​∣Di​=1]​​−never observedE[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1]​​

All of DiD is a way of imputing the second term. Equation (2) (parallel trends) and no anticipation deliver that imputation in equation (3), and equation (4) is the resulting identification formula. Choosing the ATT instead of the average effect in the whole population is what allows selection into treatment on the level of the outcome: nothing has to be assumed about Yi,2(1)Y_{i,2}(1)Yi,2​(1) for the comparison group.

Parallel trends (Assumption 1) says that, had the treatment not happened, the mean outcome of the treated population would have changed between periods 1 and 2 by the same amount as the mean outcome of the comparison population. The left side is counterfactual (it contains Yi,2(0)Y_{i,2}(0)Yi,2​(0) for treated units), the right side is identified from untreated units. The assumption restricts changes, not levels: the two groups may differ in E[Yi,t(0)∣Di=d]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,t}(0)\mid D_i=d\right]E[Yi,t​(0)∣Di​=d] by any constant.

An equivalent reading is that selection bias is constant over time. Rearranging,

E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=1]−E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=0]=E[Yi,1(0)∣Di=1]−E[Yi,1(0)∣Di=0]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=0\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=0\right]E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=0]=E[Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=0]

The model Yi,t(0)=αi+ϕt+ϵi,tY_{i,t}(0)=\alpha_i+\phi_t+\epsilon_{i,t}Yi,t​(0)=αi​+ϕt​+ϵi,t​ with E[ϵi,t∣Di]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\epsilon_{i,t}\mid D_i\right]=0E[ϵi,t​∣Di​]=0 implies it, because both sides of the equation then equal ϕ2−ϕ1\phi_2-\phi_1ϕ2​−ϕ1​. For example, if untreated means are 10 and 14 in period 1 and both would rise by 3, the assumption holds although levels differ by 4. The assumption is not invariant to transformations of the outcome: holding in levels it generally fails in logs. It is used in equation (3) to build the counterfactual, is extended to many periods in equation (8) and to covariates in equation (17), and its violation is the quantity δ1\delta_1δ1​ of equation (26).

Start from parallel trends, equation (2), and move E[Yi,1(0)∣Di=1]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]E[Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=1] to the right side:

E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=1]=E[Yi,1(0)∣Di=1]+E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=0]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=0\right]E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1]=E[Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=1]+E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=0]

The first term on the right is still counterfactual in form: treated units follow the treated path, so what is observed for them in period 1 is Yi,1(1)Y_{i,1}(1)Yi,1​(1). No anticipation (Assumption 2) states Yi,1(0)=Yi,1(1)Y_{i,1}(0)=Y_{i,1}(1)Yi,1​(0)=Yi,1​(1) for treated units, which gives the first line of the target:

E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=1]=E[Yi,1(1)∣Di=1]+E[Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)∣Di=0]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}(1)\mid D_i=1\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=0\right]E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1]=E[Yi,1​(1)∣Di​=1]+E[Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=0]

Finally use the observation rule Yi,t=DiYi,t(1)+(1−Di)Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}=D_iY_{i,t}(1)+(1-D_i)Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​=Di​Yi,t​(1)+(1−Di​)Yi,t​(0): for Di=1D_i=1Di​=1 the observed Yi,1Y_{i,1}Yi,1​ is Yi,1(1)Y_{i,1}(1)Yi,1​(1), and for Di=0D_i=0Di​=0 the observed Yi,2−Yi,1Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}Yi,2​−Yi,1​ is Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0). Substituting,

E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=1]=E[Yi,1∣Di=1]+E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0\right]E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1]=E[Yi,1​∣Di​=1]+E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0]

Only the mean version of no anticipation, E[Yi,1(0)∣Di=1]=E[Yi,1(1)∣Di=1]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}(1)\mid D_i=1\right]E[Yi,1​(0)∣Di​=1]=E[Yi,1​(1)∣Di​=1], was needed in the second step.

Begin with the definition in equation (1) and replace Yi,2(1)Y_{i,2}(1)Yi,2​(1) by the observed Yi,2Y_{i,2}Yi,2​ for treated units:

τ2=E[Yi,2∣Di=1]−E[Yi,2(0)∣Di=1]\tau_2=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]τ2​=E[Yi,2​∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,2​(0)∣Di​=1]

Insert the imputed counterfactual mean from the last line of equation (3):

τ2=E[Yi,2∣Di=1]−E[Yi,1∣Di=1]−E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0]=E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=1]−E[Yi,2−Yi,1∣Di=0]\begin{aligned} \tau_2&=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\mid D_i=0\right] \end{aligned}τ2​​=E[Yi,2​∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,1​∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0]=E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=1]−E[Yi,2​−Yi,1​∣Di​=0]​

The second line collects the two treated-group terms by linearity of the expectation. Every term is now a population mean of observed outcomes, so τ2\tau_2τ2​ is identified. Without parallel trends the same steps give the difference in differences equal to τ2+δ1\tau_2+\delta_1τ2​+δ1​, with δ1\delta_1δ1​ the difference in untreated trends defined in equation (26).

This is the plug-in (analogy) estimator of equation (4): each of the four population means is replaced by the corresponding sample mean. Y‾t=2,D=1\overline{Y}_{t=2,D=1}Yt=2,D=1​ is the average period-2 outcome of the N1N_1N1​ treated units, and similarly for the other three cells. The first bracket is the before-after change of the treated group; it mixes the treatment effect with whatever would have happened anyway. The second bracket is the before-after change of the comparison group, which under parallel trends estimates exactly that common change.

In a balanced panel the estimator can be written with unit-level changes, which is the form used for inference in equation (7):

τ^2=1N1∑i:Di=1(Yi,2−Yi,1)−1N0∑i:Di=0(Yi,2−Yi,1)\widehat{\tau}_2=\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:D_i=1}\left(Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\right)-\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i:D_i=0}\left(Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\right)τ2​=N1​1​i:Di​=1∑​(Yi,2​−Yi,1​)−N0​1​i:Di​=0∑​(Yi,2​−Yi,1​)

A numerical illustration: if the treated mean moves from 50 to 58 and the comparison mean from 40 to 43, then τ^2=8−3=5\widehat{\tau}_2=8-3=5τ2​=8−3=5. The same number is the difference between the period-2 gap (15) and the period-1 gap (10), which shows that a constant level difference between groups is harmless. The estimator equals the OLS coefficient of equation (6), and under Assumptions 1 to 3 it is consistent for τ2\tau_2τ2​ by the law of large numbers applied to the four cells.

The equation is the two-way fixed effects specification; the result to derive is that its OLS coefficient equals the DiD estimator of equation (5). With two periods, removing the unit effect by the within transformation is the same as first-differencing. Subtract the period-1 equation from the period-2 equation for unit iii; αi\alpha_iαi​ drops out and the interaction 1[t=2]⋅Di1[t=2]\cdot D_i1[t=2]⋅Di​ equals DiD_iDi​ in period 2 and zero in period 1:

Yi,2−Yi,1=(ϕ2−ϕ1)+Diβ+(ϵi,2−ϵi,1)Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}=\left(\phi_2-\phi_1\right)+D_i\beta+\left(\epsilon_{i,2}-\epsilon_{i,1}\right)Yi,2​−Yi,1​=(ϕ2​−ϕ1​)+Di​β+(ϵi,2​−ϵi,1​)

This is a cross-section regression of the change in the outcome on a constant and the binary variable DiD_iDi​. For such a regression the OLS intercept is the mean of the dependent variable in the group with Di=0D_i=0Di​=0 and the slope is the difference in group means:

β^=∑i(Di−N1/N)(Yi,2−Yi,1)∑i(Di−N1/N)2=1N1∑i:Di=1(Yi,2−Yi,1)−1N0∑i:Di=0(Yi,2−Yi,1)=τ^2\begin{aligned} \widehat{\beta}&=\frac{\sum_i\left(D_i-N_1/N\right)\left(Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\right)}{\sum_i\left(D_i-N_1/N\right)^2}\\ &=\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:D_i=1}\left(Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\right)-\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i:D_i=0}\left(Y_{i,2}-Y_{i,1}\right)=\widehat{\tau}_2 \end{aligned}β​​=∑i​(Di​−N1​/N)2∑i​(Di​−N1​/N)(Yi,2​−Yi,1​)​=N1​1​i:Di​=1∑​(Yi,2​−Yi,1​)−N0​1​i:Di​=0∑​(Yi,2​−Yi,1​)=τ2​​

The second line uses ∑i(Di−N1/N)2=N1N0/N\sum_i\left(D_i-N_1/N\right)^2=N_1N_0/N∑i​(Di​−N1​/N)2=N1​N0​/N and the fact that Di−N1/ND_i-N_1/NDi​−N1​/N equals N0/NN_0/NN0​/N for treated units and −N1/N-N_1/N−N1​/N for untreated units. Hence β^=τ^2\widehat{\beta}=\widehat{\tau}_2β​=τ2​ exactly, and by equation (4) its probability limit is τ2\tau_2τ2​. The equality relies on the balanced two-period panel with a single treatment date; with staggered timing the analogous regression, equation (9), no longer has this interpretation.

This is Assumption 4, the strongest of the staggered parallel trends assumptions. Yi,t(∞)Y_{i,t}(\infty)Yi,t​(∞) is the outcome unit iii would have in period ttt if it were never treated, and GiG_iGi​ is its first treated period. The condition requires that, for every pair of periods t≠t′t\neq t't=t′ and every pair of cohorts g≠g′g\neq g'g=g′ (the never-treated cohort g=∞g=\inftyg=∞ included), the mean never-treated outcome changes by the same amount. It is equation (2) imposed for all two-cohort, two-period combinations.

Equivalently, cohort means of the never-treated outcome are additively separable,

E[Yi,t(∞)∣Gi=g]=ag+ϕt\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i,t}(\infty)\mid G_i=g\right]=a_g+\phi_tE[Yi,t​(∞)∣Gi​=g]=ag​+ϕt​

for some cohort constants aga_gag​ and common time effects ϕt\phi_tϕt​ (take ϕt\phi_tϕt​ to be the change of any cohort's mean since period 1). This representation is what makes the TWFE regressions of equations (9) and (12) and the imputation model behind equation (16) correctly specified for untreated observations. With TTT periods and ∣G∣|\mathcal{G}|∣G∣ cohorts the assumption imposes (T−1)(∣G∣−1)(T-1)(|\mathcal{G}|-1)(T−1)(∣G∣−1) independent restrictions. Assumption 4.a keeps them only for t,t′≥gmin−1t,t'\geq g_{min}-1t,t′≥gmin​−1, which is all that equation (13) needs; a version without g=∞g=\inftyg=∞ suffices when only not-yet-treated cohorts serve as comparisons. The trade-off is that more restrictions allow more pre-treatment periods to be used (precision) but are less plausible and more exposed to bias from slowly diverging trends.

Conditional parallel trends (Assumption 6) imposes equation (2) within each covariate cell instead of in the whole population. A simple illustration: let the untreated change be 1 for units with Xi=0X_i=0Xi​=0 and 3 for units with Xi=1X_i=1Xi​=1, in both groups. If 80 percent of treated units and 20 percent of comparison units have Xi=1X_i=1Xi​=1, the unconditional trends are

The covariates must not be affected by the treatment. If XiX_iXi​ contains the lagged outcome the assumption collapses to equation (24).

These two quantities measure by how much parallel trends fails. δ1\delta_1δ1​ is the difference between the treated and comparison groups in the mean change of the untreated outcome from period 1 to period 2; equation (2) is the statement δ1=0\delta_1=0δ1​=0. δ−1\delta_{-1}δ−1​ is the same object for the pre-treatment pair of periods, written as period 0 minus period 1 so that period 1 is the reference in both. Repeating the steps of equations (3) and (4) without imposing parallel trends shows what the event-study coefficients of equations (12) and (25) estimate:

A linear difference in trends with slope κ\kappaκ per period gives δ1=κ\delta_1=\kappaδ1​=κ and δ−1=−κ\delta_{-1}=-\kappaδ−1​=−κ, hence ∣β−1∣=∣β1∣|\beta_{-1}|=|\beta_1|∣β−1​∣=∣β1​∣ when there is no effect, the case used in the low-power argument. The relative-magnitudes restriction replaces the point assumption δ1=0\delta_1=0δ1​=0 by a bound: the post-treatment violation of parallel trends is at most Mˉ\bar{M}Mˉ times the largest violation seen between consecutive pre-treatment periods. The restriction suits confounders whose shocks are of similar size before and after treatment; smoothness restrictions suit slowly evolving trends instead.

This is the design-based counterpart of parallel trends. The NNN units and their potential outcomes are fixed numbers; the only random object is the treatment vector, with πi=P(Di=1)\pi_i=P(D_i=1)πi​=P(Di​=1) the (unknown) treatment probability of unit iii and N1N_1N1​ treated units in total, so that the πi\pi_iπi​ sum to N1N_1N1​ and N1/NN_1/NN1​/N is their average. The left side is NNN times the finite-population covariance between πi\pi_iπi​ and the untreated change Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0)Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0).

The condition says that units more likely to be treated do not have systematically different untreated trends. It holds trivially under complete randomization, where πi=N1/N\pi_i=N_1/Nπi​=N1​/N for all iii, but also allows treatment probabilities to depend on anything unrelated to trends, including the level Yi,1(0)Y_{i,1}(0)Yi,1​(0). 1N1∑i=1Nπi(Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0))=1N0∑i=1N(1−πi)(Yi,2(0)−Yi,1(0))\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^N\pi_i\left(Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\right)=\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^N\left(1-\pi_i\right)\left(Y_{i,2}(0)-Y_{i,1}(0)\right)N1​1​i=1∑N​πi​(Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0))=N0​1​i=1∑N​(1−πi​)(Yi,2​(0)−Yi,1​(0))

that is, the expected average untreated trend is the same for the treated and the untreated group. Under this condition the DiD estimator of equation (5) is unbiased for the parameter in equation (33), as derived there.

The last sum is the left side of equation (32), so the bias is zero exactly when the finite-population parallel trends condition holds. The estimand weights unit effects by πi\pi_iπi​: units more likely to be treated count more, which is the finite-population meaning of "on the treated".
